section.title: The Great Commission
section.sectionRationale: The Gospel ends on a mountain in Galilee. The risen Jesus, given all authority in heaven and on earth, sends His worshiping disciples to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching, with the promise of His own presence to the end of the age.
section.thesis: The risen and enthroned Christ, holding all authority, commissions His church to make disciples of every nation by baptizing and teaching them, and He guarantees the mission with the promise of His abiding presence until the age is complete.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the eleven meeting the risen Jesus on the mountain in worship and doubt; and the commission grounded in His authority and sealed by His presence.

verses.text: Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated.
When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted.
Then Jesus came to them and said, “All {{exousia|authority}} in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.
Therefore go and {{matheteuo|make disciples}} of all {{ethne|nations}}, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

exousia.gloss: Authority, the right and power to rule. The risen Jesus declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him, the dominion of the Son of Man in Daniel 7 now His; the mission rests on His universal, sovereign lordship.

matheteuo.gloss: To make a disciple, to bring someone into committed, learning allegiance to Jesus. It is the central command of the commission: not merely to win converts but to make lifelong followers, marked by baptism and formed by obedient teaching.

ethne.gloss: Nations, peoples, the Gentiles. What was hinted throughout Matthew, the Magi, the centurion, the Canaanite woman, now becomes the explicit scope of the mission: all nations, every people group on earth, are to be discipled.

basic.context: The risen Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain in Galilee, as He had promised. They worship Him, though some still waver. He announces that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him, and on that basis He commissions them: go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything He commanded. He seals the charge with a promise: He will be with them always, to the very end of the age.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the climax and key of Matthew. Everything the Gospel has shown, Jesus' authority, His teaching, His reach toward the nations, converges here. The main command is make disciples, with going, baptizing, and teaching as its means. The Trinitarian name and the promise of Christ's presence frame the mission as the ongoing work of the whole church until He returns.
basic.originalLanguages: The risen Jesus claims all exousia, authority, in heaven and on earth. On that basis He commands His people to matheteuo, make disciples, of all the ethne, the nations, every people on earth.
basic.typology: Jesus receives the universal dominion of the Son of Man in Daniel 7. The blessing of all nations promised to Abraham reaches its fulfillment as the gospel goes to every people. The mountain recalls the mountains of revelation throughout Matthew.
basic.christ: Jesus is the risen, enthroned Lord with all authority, the one baptized into whose name people belong to God, the teacher whose commands are to be obeyed, and the ever-present Immanuel, God with us to the end of the age.
basic.god: God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is named as the one God into whose name disciples are baptized. God's ancient purpose to bless all nations is now unleashed, and He commits Himself, in Christ, to be present with His people as they carry it out.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man's universal dominion. Genesis 12 promises blessing to all nations through Abraham. Matthew 1 opened with Immanuel, God with us, now fulfilled in the closing promise. Acts 1 sends the church as witnesses to the ends of the earth.
basic.oneStory: The Gospel that began with Immanuel, God with us, ends with the risen Christ promising, I am with you always. All authority is His, the nations are His field, and His presence is His people's power. The story of the kingdom, from Abraham's promised blessing to the nations to the enthroned Son of Man, now becomes the church's mission, and it runs on to the end of the age, when the King who commissions will come again.

context.literary:
The last five verses of Matthew are built as a small drama in three movements: arrival, speech, promise. The eleven go, they see, they worship, verses 16 and 17. Jesus comes to them and speaks, verses 18 to 20a. Then comes one sentence that looks forward rather than back, verse 20b. Nearly everything in the speech has been prepared by earlier pages. The mountain, the Galilee setting, the word for 'nations', the name 'with us' and the teaching of commands each return from the opening and the middle of the Gospel, so that the ending reads like a gathering of threads.

The speech itself has a clear shape. It opens with a statement, 'All authority ... has been given to Me', and the word 'Therefore' hangs the whole commission on that statement. Then comes one command surrounded by participles. In the Greek the only imperative is 'make disciples'. 'Going', 'baptizing' and 'teaching' are participles that say how the one task is carried out. The commission closes with 'Behold, I am with you', which echoes the opening promise of Matthew 1:23, 'God with us'. Many readers see an inclusio, with the Gospel framed from first to last by the presence of God in Jesus.

The narrator also does something rare. He ends without an ascension scene. Luke and Acts describe Jesus being taken up; Matthew leaves Him standing on the mountain, still speaking, still present. The Gospel closes in mid-mission, which suits its message: the story of Jesus does not end here but is carried on by the people He addresses, with Him alongside them. The mention of doubt in verse 17 is equally deliberate. Matthew does not tidy the eleven into a flawless group before commissioning them.
context.historical:
Matthew's Gospel was written to a community deeply rooted in Jewish Scripture and practice, and also open to the outsider, as the visit of the Magi in Matthew 2:1 to 12 and the faith of the centurion in Matthew 8:5 to 13 already showed. The commission fits that world. Galilee had been called 'Galilee of the Gentiles' in Matthew 4:15, quoting Isaiah 9:1 to 2, a region of mixed population at the northern edge of Israel, far from the Jerusalem establishment. The risen Lord chooses that region for His meeting with the eleven, just as the angel and Jesus Himself said He would, Matthew 26:32 and 28:7 and 10.

The eleven themselves are a stunned and shrunken company. One of the Twelve has died by his own hand, Matthew 27:5. They had scattered when Jesus was arrested, Matthew 26:56. Their first reaction to the empty tomb had been rumour and fear, and the chief priests had circulated a counter story that the disciples stole the body, Matthew 28:11 to 15. Matthew notes that this story 'has been circulated among the Jews to this very day', verse 15, which tells us he is writing some time after the events and with a live dispute in view.

Baptism was no novelty. Jewish washings, the baptism of proselytes who joined Israel from the nations, and above all John's baptism of repentance in the Jordan all formed the background, Matthew 3:5 to 6. What is new is the name into which baptism is performed. A Jewish hearer knew that Israel's confession was that the LORD is one, Deuteronomy 6:4. To be baptized 'in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit' placed Jesus and the Spirit within that one divine name, and it set a mission directed to the nations, the very people for whom Israel's Scriptures had long said light would come.
context.canonical:
Matthew 28:16 to 20 gathers promises from across the Old Testament. The Daniel 7 background is the most direct. There 'One like the Son of Man' is led into the presence of the Ancient of Days and 'was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him', Daniel 7:13 to 14. The phrase 'has been given' in Matthew 28:18 renews that scene, and Jesus has used Son of Man language of Himself all through the Gospel, for example Matthew 26:64.

The other great background is the promise to Abraham. God told him in Genesis 12:3 that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you', and the same vision carries through the Psalms and the prophets. The nations 'will remember and turn to the LORD', Psalm 22:27, and 'many nations will join themselves to the LORD', Zechariah 2:11. The Servant of Isaiah would be 'a light for the nations', Isaiah 49:6, and Matthew has already read that Servant in Jesus, Matthew 12:18 to 21. Isaiah 66:18 to 19 even pictures survivors sent out to the nations who 'have not heard of My fame'.

Later Scripture shows the commission being obeyed. Acts 1:8 repeats it with the Spirit's power, and Luke 24:46 to 48 gives the same charge in other words. Paul says the mystery hidden for ages is now made known 'to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith', Romans 16:25 to 26, which is a close echo of 'teaching them to obey'. Acts 14:21 describes a team that 'made many disciples'. And the vision of Revelation 7:9, a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue', is the commission fully answered.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants his readers to finish the Gospel knowing what kind of people they now are. They are not an audience who have heard an account of a past teacher. They are the people whom the risen Lord commissions, and the Gospel has been training them for the task. That is why the closing speech is so full of teaching words. The five great discourses of the book, from the Sermon on the Mount to the Olivet teaching, were not decoration; they are the 'all that I have commanded' that disciples are now to pass on.

He also means the reader to settle the question of authority before anything else. Early in the Gospel the crowds were amazed that Jesus taught 'as one who had authority', Matthew 7:29. Now the risen Jesus tells them where that authority comes from and how far it reaches. Because it is complete, the mission can reach everywhere, and because it is His, the mission can be trusted.

Finally Matthew means to give comfort to a church that is weak, doubting and small. Verse 17 is not an embarrassing leftover. It tells every later disciple that Jesus sends out people whose faith is real but unfinished, and that His promise of presence is meant for exactly those people.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage is plainly prescriptive. Jesus gives a command, make disciples, and says how: baptize, and teach obedience. Those instructions are addressed first to the eleven but they were understood from the start to belong to the whole church, since the work was to run 'to the end of the age', which is far longer than the eleven could live. The earliest Christians treated it that way, as Acts shows.

Care is still needed in applying it. The statement 'All authority ... has been given to Me' describes what is true of Jesus; it is not handed to the church as its own. The church goes in His authority, never in a power of its own, and it has no licence to use force or coercion, since the method is teaching and baptizing. The detail that the eleven went to a particular mountain in Galilee is description, not a rule about where mission must begin. Nor should anyone take 'I am with you always' as a promise that every plan will succeed. It is a promise of His company, which Matthew has already shown to include suffering, as in Matthew 10:16 to 25, and not an exemption from it.

debates.question: Does 'all the nations' include Israel, or only the Gentiles?

views.label: All peoples, Israel included
views.case: The Greek ethne can mean 'Gentiles' or simply 'nations', and the word 'all' sits in front of it. Earlier in the Gospel Jesus had told the Twelve to avoid Gentile roads and go to 'the lost sheep of Israel', Matthew 10:5 to 6. That earlier limit is now lifted, but Israel is not set aside. In Matthew 24:14 and 25:32 the same phrase evidently takes in everyone, Jews as well as others, and the first disciples in Acts preached to Jews first, Acts 2:38. On this view the commission widens the mission rather than redirecting it.

views.label: The Gentile nations specifically
views.case: In Matthew 10:18 the same word ethne is rendered 'Gentiles' and plainly means non-Jews, and in Matthew 4:15 it is 'Galilee of the Gentiles'. Some argue that the verse therefore turns from the Jewish mission of Matthew 10 to a Gentile one, so that the commission is the lifting of the earlier restriction toward the outside world, not a new instruction about Israel.

debates.bearing: The two readings differ less than they first seem. Both agree that the restriction of Matthew 10:5 to 6 is now over and that no people is outside the reach of the Great Commission. The practical result for the church is the same: it goes to every people, including the one it belongs to, and it does not treat any ethnic group as a closed door.

debates.question: Who were the 'some' who doubted, and what does the doubt mean?

views.label: Some of the eleven
views.case: The sentence in verse 17 speaks of the eleven who 'saw Him', worshiped, and 'some doubted'. On the plainest reading all the subjects belong to one group. Matthew uses the verb of Peter sinking, Matthew 14:31, where it describes a believer whose trust wavers, not an unbeliever. So the doubt is hesitation or uncertainty, not rejection.

views.label: Others present beside the eleven
views.case: Some suggest a larger group was on the mountain, since Paul speaks of more than five hundred who saw the risen Christ at once, 1 Corinthians 15:6. Matthew, however, names only the eleven in verse 16, and the commission is addressed to the group he has just described, so this reading must supply a crowd the text does not mention.

debates.bearing: Whoever the doubters were, Jesus does not withdraw the commission and does not wait for certainty. He comes toward them, 'Then Jesus came to them', verse 18, and speaks. The lesson for readers is that unfinished faith is no disqualification and that the cure for doubt is the presence and word of the risen Lord, not a stronger grip on one's own conviction.

study.originalLanguages:
The structure of the commission is easy to miss in English, where 'go', 'make disciples', 'baptizing' and 'teaching' look like four commands. In the Greek there is one imperative, matheteusate, 'make disciples'. 'Go' is a participle, poreuthentes, 'having gone' or 'as you go', and it presupposes movement rather than commanding it. 'Baptizing' and 'teaching' are present participles, baptizontes and didaskontes, which describe how disciple making happens and are continuing activities, not one-off acts. The grammar puts the weight on the single task of producing disciples, learners who belong to Jesus, and treats going, baptizing and teaching as the means.

The verb matheteuo is rare and Matthew is nearly its only user in the Gospels. He uses it of a scribe who has been 'discipled in the kingdom of heaven', Matthew 13:52, and of Joseph of Arimathea, 'who himself was a disciple of Jesus', Matthew 27:57. Luke later uses it in Acts 14:21, 'made many disciples'. A disciple here is a learner who attaches himself to a master, which explains why the commission continues straight into baptism and teaching.

The baptism is 'into the name', eis to onoma, using a preposition of movement into and not simply 'in'. The preposition suggests allegiance, belonging to the one whose name is spoken. The word 'name' is singular, though three persons follow: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The singular is the grammar of one God with three persons, and Matthew does not stop to explain it, which suggests his readers already took it for granted. Compare 2 Corinthians 13:14 and the Spirit and Father together in Matthew 3:16 to 17.

The word 'teaching' is followed by terein, 'to keep' or 'to guard', in the phrase 'to obey all that I have commanded you'. The sense is of guarding something carefully and holding it, so that hearing becomes doing, as at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew 7:24 to 27. The scope is 'all', panta hosa, everything He has commanded, not a convenient selection.

The promise, ego meth' hymon eimi, 'I am with you', puts the personal pronoun in front, which gives it emphasis, and 'always' is literally 'all the days', pasas tas hemeras. It means every day, including the dark ones. The 'end of the age' translates synteleia tou aionos, a phrase Matthew uses for the harvest and the final reckoning, Matthew 13:39 and 24:3. And the verb in verse 18, 'has been given', edothe, is an aorist passive. It is the grammar of a gift from God, and in Daniel 7:14 in the Greek translation the very same verb stands in the same position: authority 'was given' to the Son of Man.

typology.fulfillment: Matthew has consistently set decisive moments on mountains. The tempter offers the kingdoms from a mountain, Matthew 4:8 to 10; Jesus teaches from a mountain, Matthew 5:1; and He is transfigured on a high mountain, Matthew 17:1 to 5, where the Father's voice says 'Listen to Him!' Moses received the law at Sinai, Exodus 19:20. The mountain of the commission completes the pattern. The Son who was shown in glory is now enthroned and speaks as the new Lawgiver whose commands the nations are to keep. The correspondence is of place and role, not of landscape; no particular peak is named, and the point is that the authority which met Israel at Sinai now goes out to the world.

typology.type: The Son of Man receiving dominion
typology.fulfillment: Daniel's vision shows a figure led before the Ancient of Days and given 'dominion, glory, and kingship', Daniel 7:14. Jesus told the high priest that he would see the Son of Man 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven', Matthew 26:64. On the mountain the vision has begun to be real, and Jesus speaks from the position of one who has received everything. The type is still unfolding in one respect: Daniel's figure is served by every nation, and the commission is the means by which people from every nation are now brought to serve Him, until the full scene of Revelation 7:9 is seen.

God's promise that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed' through Abraham, Genesis 12:3, was a seed sown at the start of the story. Matthew opens by naming Jesus 'the son of Abraham', Matthew 1:1, and closes by sending His disciples to every nation. Paul explains that this is how the promise is kept: those baptized into Christ are 'Abraham's seed and heirs according to the promise', Galatians 3:27 to 29, whatever their background. The promise to one family was always about the many. The difference is that Abraham was a pilgrim in one land, and the commission sends the blessing to every land.

From the tabernacle onward God had promised to dwell among His people, Exodus 25:8, and the prophets spoke of Immanuel. The promise of presence given to Joshua, 'the LORD your God is with you wherever you go', Joshua 1:9, was given for a single campaign. In Matthew 28:20 the same presence is promised to a worldwide and age-long mission, and it is the presence of Jesus Himself, not of an angel or a symbol. The type falls short only in that Joshua's promise was tied to a land, while this one has no boundary and no end date short of the close of the age.

study.christ:
This final scene answers the question the whole Gospel has been asking: who is this? Matthew has shown Him as the child with the name 'Jesus', who 'will save His people from their sins', Matthew 1:21, as Immanuel, as the Servant who brings justice to the nations, Matthew 12:18 to 21, and as the Son whom the Father loves, Matthew 3:17. In chapter 28 all of these meet in one figure standing on a mountain with every kind of authority in His hands.

First, He is the resurrected Lord. The authority He claims was given to Him after the cross, and it is the answer of the Father to the shame of Good Friday. Paul describes the same exaltation: God 'exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names', Philippians 2:9 to 11, and seated Him 'far above all rule and authority, power and dominion', Ephesians 1:20 to 21. Jesus claims what Satan once offered falsely in the temptation, Matthew 4:8 to 9, but He receives it from the Father by way of obedience and the cross, not by worship of the devil.

Second, He is the one to whom worship is rightly given. The eleven 'worshiped Him', verse 17, and Jesus does not correct them, though angels and apostles refuse worship when it is offered to them elsewhere. Matthew has used the same verb for the Magi at the manger, Matthew 2:11, and for the disciples in the boat who confessed Him as Son of God, Matthew 14:33. The Gospel ends where it began, with people on their knees before Jesus.

Third, He is the teacher whose words carry divine weight. 'All that I have commanded you' places His commandments alongside the law of God. In the Sermon on the Mount He had said 'You have heard that it was said ... but I tell you', and He had said that those who practice and teach His commands will be great in the kingdom, Matthew 5:19. The disciples are not told to pass on their own insights, nor even the best of tradition. They are told to pass on what Jesus commanded.

Finally, He is Immanuel. The promise 'I am with you always' fulfils the name given at the start of the Gospel, 'God with us', Matthew 1:23. The one who made that promise has died and risen, so His presence is no longer tied to a village in Galilee. Elsewhere He said that where two or three gather in His name He is among them, Matthew 18:20. He is not a ruler who delegates and leaves; He leads the mission from within it. It is also worth guarding against forced readings: the mountain is not a secret code for Sinai or Zion, and the passage does not need one. Its Christology is stated plainly in the speech itself.
study.god:
The commission shows the one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and it does so in the ordinary language of worship rather than in a lecture. The disciples are baptized into one name, singular, yet three are named. Matthew had already shown the three together at Jesus' baptism, with the Father's voice, the Son in the water and the Spirit descending like a dove, Matthew 3:16 to 17. In chapter 28 that pattern becomes the identity into which every new disciple is placed. To belong to God is to belong to this threefold name.

It shows God as the sovereign who has given authority to the Son. The word 'given' says that the Father has acted. Jesus said earlier, 'All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father', Matthew 11:27, and John's Gospel says that the Father granted Him 'authority over all people', John 17:2. The God of the passage is therefore not remote. He has installed His Son as the Lord of heaven and earth, and He stands behind the commission. This holds together the unity of God, since the one name is spoken, and the distinct roles of Father and Son, since one gives and the other receives.

It shows God as faithful to His ancient promise. The blessing He pledged to Abraham for all the families of the earth, Genesis 12:3, did not lapse during the long centuries of Israel's history, and the prophets repeated it with growing detail, from Isaiah 2:2 to 3 to Isaiah 49:6. The commission is God keeping a promise made before Israel had a king. His purposes include the nations from the beginning, and Romans 16:25 to 26 calls this a mystery 'concealed for ages past' but now made known.

It shows God as present. In the Old Testament God's 'I will be with you' was given to Moses, Exodus 3:12, to Joshua, to Israel in exile, Isaiah 41:10, and always attached to a specific task or crisis. Here it is attached to the largest task imaginable and to every day of it. The same writer who opened with 'God with us' now closes with God's presence guaranteed in the person of the risen Jesus, and the Hebrews' promise that God will 'never leave' His people, Hebrews 13:5, is its echo.

For worship, the passage teaches that doubt and adoration can stand side by side in the same room and that God accepts both without waiting for the doubt to clear. It also teaches that worship and mission are not rivals. The disciples who fall down in verse 17 are the ones sent out in verse 19, and mission that does not begin in worship will lose its direction, while worship that never moves toward the nations has misunderstood the God it worships.

crossReferences.note: The Son of Man is led before the Ancient of Days and 'was given dominion, glory, and kingship, that the people of every nation and language should serve Him.' The phrase 'has been given' in Matthew 28:18 renews this scene, and the 'every nation' of Daniel is the 'all nations' of the commission.

God promises Abraham that 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you.' Matthew opens with Jesus as son of Abraham and closes by sending disciples to every nation, so the end of the Gospel is the long answer to the call that began Israel's story.

'They will call Him Immanuel,' which means 'God with us.' The promise 'I am with you always' in 28:20 closes the Gospel on the same note it began with. The child born as God with us now remains with His people to the end of the age.

The Twelve were first sent only 'to the lost sheep of Israel' and told to avoid Gentile roads. The earlier limit prepared the ground, and the later widening to all nations in chapter 28 shows that the order, Israel first and then every people, was part of the plan.

The Servant is told it is 'not enough' only to restore Israel; He will be 'a light for the nations' bringing salvation 'to the ends of the earth.' Matthew has applied the Servant songs to Jesus, so the commission is that light being carried out through those who follow Him.

The risen Jesus promises power when the Spirit comes and sends the apostles as witnesses 'to the ends of the earth.' It puts the same commission in a geographic order, from Jerusalem outward, and supplies what Matthew's ending leaves implied, the Spirit's power.

Luke records the same charge in different words: repentance and forgiveness 'will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem.' Set beside Matthew it shows that the substance of the commission, a message of forgiveness proclaimed in the Messiah's name, was remembered in more than one form.

Paul explains what baptism means: believers are 'baptized into Christ Jesus', into His death, and raised to walk in newness of life. It fills in the 'baptizing them' of Matthew 28:19 and shows that baptism is a sharing in the cross and resurrection, not only an outward rite.

God exalted Jesus 'to the highest place' so that every knee bows to Him. This is the same authority that Matthew 28:18 records in the Lord's own words, and Paul looks to the day when every tongue confesses what the disciples on the mountain already did.

John sees 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' before the throne. The commission to all nations finds its goal here, in a worshiping crowd drawn from every people the disciples were first sent to.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible begins with a human family, a command to fill the earth, and a world that belongs to God, Genesis 1:28. Sin breaks that world apart, and Genesis 11 shows the nations scattered at Babel, divided by language and pride. The call of Abraham in Genesis 12 is God's answer to that scattering: out of one family He will bless 'all the families of the earth'. The rest of the Old Testament is that promise passing through Israel, held back by Israel's own failures, and held open by the prophets who see the nations coming to the mountain of the LORD, Isaiah 2:2 to 3, and see a Servant who is a light to the ends of the earth, Isaiah 49:6.

Matthew 28 is where the promise is set in motion for the first time as a mission. The Son of Man has died for sins, risen, and received dominion over everything. The people He had gathered, small, doubtful and afraid, are now sent to the very nations from which Abraham's family had been separated. Pentecost follows and Acts traces the first stretch of the journey, from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and on towards the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8. Babel's scattered nations are now to be gathered, and the barriers of language and ethnicity that sin had raised are crossed by the gospel. Paul calls the unity this creates a new humanity in which there is 'neither Jew nor Greek', Galatians 3:28.

The passage also answers a lingering worry in the story. Israel had often failed to carry God's light to the world, and the exile seemed to prove that the promise had stalled. The commission shows that God was never dependent on Israel's strength. The one faithful Israelite has done what Israel could not, and now He brings others into His own obedience, as the final line says: 'teaching them to obey'.

The story ends where Matthew's commission says it will, at the 'end of the age'. Jesus will return as the King who commissions. The vision of Revelation 7:9, with people from every nation and tongue before the Lamb, shows the commission completed. The tree of life is again offered, the nations walk by the light of God's presence, Revelation 21:24, and God dwells with His people, the Immanuel promise at last made complete, Revelation 21:3. Until then, every congregation that baptizes a new disciple and teaches them to keep His words is taking a small step in the movement that Genesis 12 began.

quiz.q: On what basis does Jesus give the Great Commission?

options.text: On His own all-encompassing authority in heaven and on earth as the risen Lord.
options.note: Verse 18 grounds the therefore of the commission in Christ's universal authority.

options.text: On the disciples' readiness and strong faith.
options.note: Some even doubted; the commission rests on Christ's authority, not the disciples' strength.

options.text: On the size and influence of the early church.
options.note: The eleven were a small, broken band; the basis is Christ's authority, not their numbers.

options.text: On the permission granted by the authorities.
options.note: The authority is Christ's own, given by God, not granted by any human power.

quiz.q: What is the central command of the Great Commission?

options.text: To make disciples of all nations, through going, baptizing, and teaching.
options.note: Make disciples is the main command, with the other actions as its means.

options.text: To travel widely and preach to as many as possible.
options.note: Going is part of it, but the goal is making disciples, not travel or preaching alone.

options.text: To baptize as many people as can be found.
options.note: Baptizing is a means; the aim is committed disciples, formed also by teaching.

options.text: To wait in Jerusalem for the nations to come.
options.note: The command is to go to all nations, not to wait for them.

quiz.q: Into whose name are disciples to be baptized?

options.text: The one name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.
options.note: Verse 19 gives the Trinitarian baptismal name, one name for the three persons.
Baptism is into the triune name here; the single name embraces Father, Son, and Spirit together.

options.text: The names of the apostles who baptize them.
options.note: Baptism is into God's name, not the apostles'.
Jesus specifies the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

quiz.q: What promise seals the Great Commission?

options.text: Jesus' abiding presence: surely I am with you always, to the end of the age.
options.note: Verse 20 closes with Christ's promise of continual presence.

options.text: That the mission will be easy and free of opposition.
options.note: He promises His presence, not the absence of hardship, which this misstates.

options.text: That the disciples will see quick and total success.
options.note: The promise is His presence through the whole age, not guaranteed instant results.

options.text: That the task will be finished within their lifetime.
options.note: He promises to be with them to the end of the age, implying a long mission.

questions: Some worshiped and some doubted, yet Jesus commissioned them all. How does it encourage you that Christ uses imperfect, sometimes doubting disciples for His mission?
The command is to make disciples, not merely to gain decisions. Whom is God calling you to help grow into a lifelong follower of Jesus?
The mission reaches all nations. How does the global scope of Christ's purpose stretch your vision beyond your own circle?
Jesus grounds the mission in His authority and seals it with His presence. Where do you need to trust that He goes with you into a hard obedience?
The Gospel ends with I am with you always. How would living each day conscious of the present, risen Christ change the way you follow Him?

translationNotes.note: But some doubted may mean some among the eleven wavered, or some hesitated before recognizing Him; Matthew records honest human frailty even in the moment of worship.

Go is literally a participle, having gone; make disciples is the main imperative, with going, baptizing, and teaching describing how disciples are made. The name is singular for the three persons, a witness to the Trinity.
The end of the age looks to the consummation Jesus described in the Olivet Discourse; the promise of His presence spans the whole mission until He returns, echoing Immanuel in Matthew 1:23.
